I'm 62 this year, and I've been farming in Quzhou County for over four decades. I finished senior high school, which around here makes me one of the more book-learned farmers, so I pay attention to the agricultural extension bulletins and soil test reports. I don't chase risky crops like some of the younger farmers trying vegetables or stevia — at my age, stability matters more than speculation. My land is 8 mu, and I've kept it in the wheat-maize double cropping rotation for years. It's reliable, and I know these fields well.

Right now it's early spring, and my winter wheat — shimai22, an improved variety — is greening up after winter dormancy. I rotary-tilled the soil before sowing last October, and the stand looks uniform. This year I'll irrigate four times: revival water, jointing, flowering, and grain filling. Pumping costs keep rising, but skimping on water at jointing is false economy. For fertilizer, I'm applying 20 kg of nitrogen per mu, split between basal dressing and a topdress at jointing, plus 6 kg of phosphorus and 4 kg of potassium per mu to maintain the nutrient balance. I'll spray pesticides three times — herbicide once, plus fungicide and insecticide as needed. If the spring weather cooperates, I expect about 1,050 kg per mu.

After wheat harvest in early June, I'll immediately plant denghai605 hybrid maize using no-tillage. The window is only about a week, so there's no time to plough. I'll apply 18 kg N, 5 kg P, and 4 kg K per mu for the maize, irrigate twice depending on summer rainfall, and spray three times for weed and pest control. Barring disasters, I should get around 1,250 kg per mu from the maize.
